title: Functional Analysis
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 400L Functional Analysis curriculum: normed and Banach spaces, inner product and Hilbert spaces, bounded linear operators and functionals, the major structural theorems (Hahn-Banach, Open Mapping, Closed Graph, Uniform Boundedness), orthogonality and the Riesz representation theorem, and an introduction to spectral and compact operator theory.

questions.question: A normed space is a vector space X equipped with a function ||.|| satisfying:
questions.explanation: These are the three defining norm axioms: positive definiteness, absolute homogeneity, and the triangle inequality.

questions.question: A Banach space is defined as:
options: A vector space with an inner product only
questions.explanation: Completeness means every Cauchy sequence in the space converges to a limit within the space.

questions.question: A Hilbert space is defined as:
options: Any vector space with a norm
questions.explanation: A Hilbert space is an inner product space that is complete with respect to the norm induced by the inner product.

questions.question: Every inner product space induces a norm defined by:
questions.explanation: This is the standard norm induced by an inner product, which can be shown to satisfy all norm axioms.

questions.question: The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality in an inner product space states that:
questions.explanation: This fundamental inequality bounds the inner product of two vectors by the product of their norms, with equality iff the vectors are linearly dependent.

questions.question: The parallelogram law ||x+y||^2 + ||x-y||^2 = 2||x||^2 + 2||y||^2 holds:
options: In every inner product space, and characterizes norms that come from an inner product
In every normed space, without exception
Only when x and y are orthogonal
questions.correct_answer: In every inner product space, and characterizes norms that come from an inner product
questions.explanation: By the Jordan-von Neumann theorem, a norm satisfying the parallelogram law is precisely one that arises from an inner product.

questions.question: The space l^2 of square-summable sequences, with norm ||x|| = (sum of |x_n|^2)^(1/2), is an example of a:
questions.explanation: l^2 is complete under its natural norm and the norm arises from an inner product, making it a canonical infinite-dimensional Hilbert space.
questions.topic: Examples of Banach and Hilbert spaces

questions.question: The space C[a,b] of continuous functions on [a,b] with the sup norm ||f|| = sup|f(x)| is:
options: A Banach space but not a Hilbert space under this norm
questions.correct_answer: A Banach space but not a Hilbert space under this norm
questions.explanation: C[a,b] is complete under the sup norm, but this norm does not satisfy the parallelogram law, so it is not induced by an inner product.
questions.topic: Examples of Banach and Hilbert spaces

questions.question: A linear operator T: X to Y between normed spaces is said to be bounded if there exists M >= 0 such that:
options: ||Tx|| <= M ||x|| for all x in X
questions.correct_answer: ||Tx|| <= M ||x|| for all x in X
questions.explanation: This inequality defines a bounded linear operator, meaning it cannot amplify the norm of a vector by more than a fixed factor M.

questions.question: For linear operators between normed spaces, boundedness is equivalent to:
questions.explanation: For linear maps between normed spaces, boundedness and continuity are equivalent properties.

questions.question: The operator norm of a bounded linear operator T is defined as:
questions.explanation: This is the smallest constant M for which the boundedness inequality ||Tx|| <= M||x|| holds for all x.

questions.question: The dual space X* of a normed space X consists of:
options: All bounded (continuous) linear functionals on X
All linear operators from X to X
questions.correct_answer: All bounded (continuous) linear functionals on X
questions.explanation: The dual space is the space of continuous scalar-valued linear maps on X, itself a normed (in fact Banach) space under the operator norm.

questions.question: The Hahn-Banach theorem guarantees that:
options: A bounded linear functional defined on a subspace can be extended to the whole space without increasing its norm
Every space is a Hilbert space
questions.correct_answer: A bounded linear functional defined on a subspace can be extended to the whole space without increasing its norm
questions.explanation: This extension theorem is one of the cornerstone results of functional analysis, underpinning duality theory.

questions.question: One important consequence of the Hahn-Banach theorem is that:
options: The dual space of a nontrivial normed space contains enough functionals to separate points
Every linear functional is automatically bounded
questions.correct_answer: The dual space of a nontrivial normed space contains enough functionals to separate points
questions.explanation: Hahn-Banach guarantees that for any nonzero x, there exists a bounded functional f with f(x) not equal to zero, so functionals separate distinct points.

questions.question: The Open Mapping Theorem states that a bounded linear surjective operator between Banach spaces:
options: Maps open sets to open sets
Maps closed sets to open sets only
questions.correct_answer: Maps open sets to open sets
questions.explanation: Completeness of both spaces is essential to this theorem, which fails in general incomplete normed spaces.

questions.question: A corollary of the Open Mapping Theorem is the Bounded Inverse Theorem, which states that a bijective bounded linear operator between Banach spaces has:
questions.explanation: Since the operator maps open sets to open sets, its set-theoretic inverse is automatically continuous, i.e. bounded.

questions.question: The Closed Graph Theorem states that a linear operator T: X to Y between Banach spaces is bounded if and only if:
options: Its graph {(x, Tx) : x in X} is closed in X times Y
questions.correct_answer: Its graph {(x, Tx) : x in X} is closed in X times Y
questions.explanation: This theorem lets one verify boundedness by checking a closedness condition on the graph, often easier than a direct estimate.

questions.question: The Uniform Boundedness Principle (Banach-Steinhaus theorem) states that a family of bounded linear operators on a Banach space that is pointwise bounded is:
questions.explanation: Pointwise boundedness for every x, combined with completeness (via the Baire Category Theorem), forces a uniform bound on the operator norms.

questions.question: Two vectors x, y in an inner product space are said to be orthogonal if:
questions.explanation: Orthogonality is defined directly by the vanishing of the inner product.

questions.question: An orthonormal set {e_n} in a Hilbert space satisfies:
options: <e_i,e_j> = 0 for i not equal to j, and ||e_i|| = 1 for all i
questions.correct_answer: <e_i,e_j> = 0 for i not equal to j, and ||e_i|| = 1 for all i
questions.explanation: This combines pairwise orthogonality with unit norm, the defining property of an orthonormal set.

questions.question: Parseval's identity for an orthonormal basis {e_n} of a Hilbert space H states that for x in H:
questions.explanation: Parseval's identity expresses the norm of x entirely in terms of its Fourier-type coefficients with respect to the orthonormal basis.

questions.question: The Riesz Representation Theorem for Hilbert spaces states that every bounded linear functional f on a Hilbert space H can be represented as:
options: f(x) = <x,y> for a unique y in H
f(x) = x for a scalar x
questions.correct_answer: f(x) = <x,y> for a unique y in H
questions.explanation: This theorem identifies the dual of a Hilbert space with the space itself via the inner product.

questions.question: The orthogonal projection theorem states that for a closed subspace M of a Hilbert space H, every x in H can be uniquely written as:
options: x = m + n where m is in M and n is in the orthogonal complement of M
x = m only, with m in M
x is never decomposable in this way
x = m times n for m in M
questions.correct_answer: x = m + n where m is in M and n is in the orthogonal complement of M
questions.explanation: This decomposition exists and is unique precisely because M is a closed subspace of a Hilbert space.

questions.question: A linear operator T on a Hilbert space is called self-adjoint if:
questions.explanation: This is the defining property of a self-adjoint (Hermitian) operator, equal to its own adjoint.

questions.question: The spectrum of a bounded linear operator T on a Banach space consists of all scalars lambda such that:
options: T minus lambda times the identity is not invertible (as a bounded operator)
T equals lambda times the identity
questions.correct_answer: T minus lambda times the identity is not invertible (as a bounded operator)
questions.explanation: The spectrum generalizes the notion of eigenvalue and includes values where T minus lambda I fails to have a bounded inverse.

questions.question: Every eigenvalue of an operator T lies in the spectrum of T, but in infinite dimensions the spectrum may also contain:
options: Values that are not eigenvalues, arising from the continuous or residual spectrum
questions.correct_answer: Values that are not eigenvalues, arising from the continuous or residual spectrum
questions.explanation: Unlike the finite-dimensional case, the spectrum of an infinite-dimensional operator can strictly contain the set of eigenvalues.

questions.question: A compact linear operator T: X to Y is one for which:
options: The image of every bounded set has compact closure in Y
T is always the identity operator
questions.correct_answer: The image of every bounded set has compact closure in Y
questions.explanation: Compact operators send bounded sets to relatively compact sets, a stronger property than mere boundedness.

questions.question: Every compact operator on an infinite-dimensional normed space is necessarily:
questions.explanation: Compactness is a stronger condition than boundedness, so every compact operator is in particular bounded.

questions.question: In a finite-dimensional normed space, all norms are:
questions.explanation: On a finite-dimensional vector space, any two norms induce the same topology and are related by fixed positive constants.

questions.question: In a finite-dimensional normed space, a subset is compact if and only if it is:
questions.explanation: This is the Heine-Borel property, which holds in finite dimensions but fails in general infinite-dimensional normed spaces.

questions.question: A sequence (x_n) in a normed space converges weakly to x if:
options: f(x_n) tends to f(x) for every bounded linear functional f
x_n = x for all large n
questions.correct_answer: f(x_n) tends to f(x) for every bounded linear functional f
questions.explanation: Weak convergence is defined via testing against all elements of the dual space, rather than requiring norm convergence.

questions.question: Strong (norm) convergence in a normed space always implies:
options: The reverse implication: weak implies strong always
questions.explanation: If ||x_n - x|| tends to 0, then for any bounded functional f, |f(x_n)-f(x)| <= ||f|| ||x_n-x|| tends to 0, so strong convergence implies weak convergence.
